nameStory: The "Jelly" part of this fungus's name comes from its distinctive gelatinous, squishy texture that feels like a gummy candy when you gently squeeze it. The "Club" describes its overall shape - a thick stem topped with an irregularly rounded head, like a tiny, colorful club sprouting from the forest floor. Some people also call them "jelly babies" after the popular British gummy candies they resemble!
description: Ochre Jelly Clubs are small, distinctive fungi that look like tiny orange-brown clubs poking up from the forest floor. They grow up to about 2½ inches tall, with a thick stem supporting an irregularly shaped, rounded head. The entire mushroom has a unique gelatinous, rubbery texture and displays beautiful ochre (golden-orange) colors often tinged with olive-green. You'll typically find them growing in clusters, creating colorful patches among the moss and leaf litter.

idTips.label: Gelatinous texture
idTips.description: The entire mushroom feels rubbery and gelatinous when gently squeezed, like a firm gummy candy - this squishy texture is unmistakable

idTips.label: Club-shaped form
idTips.description: Distinctive shape with a thick stem topped by an irregularly rounded, brain-like head that's clearly separated from the stalk

idTips.label: Ochre coloration
idTips.description: Rich golden-orange (ochre) color throughout, often with subtle olive-green tints, especially on the fertile head portion

idTips.label: Clustered growth
idTips.description: Usually grows in groups or tight clusters rather than individually, creating colorful patches on the forest floor

idTips.label: Smooth, moist surface
idTips.description: The surface feels smooth and slightly moist to the touch, never dry or powdery like many other fungi

habitat: Look for Ochre Jelly Clubs in moist, shaded woodlands throughout New England, especially in areas with rich organic soil and plenty of moss. They thrive among decaying leaves, fallen logs, and plant debris in both deciduous and mixed forests. You'll often find them in the same areas where you might spot other small woodland fungi, particularly in spots that stay consistently damp.

seasonality.spring: Not typically visible in early spring as they prefer warmer, more consistently moist conditions.
seasonality.summer: Begin appearing in mid to late summer when woodland moisture levels are high and temperatures are warm but not extreme.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for fruiting, when you're most likely to find fresh, vibrant specimens among the fallen leaves and increased forest moisture.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies disappear with cold weather, leaving no visible trace above ground until the next growing season.

funFact: Despite their candy-like appearance and "jelly baby" nickname, these fungi might actually be helping nearby trees survive by forming beneficial partnerships with their roots - they could be trading nutrients with living trees while also decomposing dead organic matter, essentially working two jobs in the forest ecosystem!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative Chicken Lips (Leotia viscosa), but Chicken Lips are more yellow-green while Ochre Jelly Clubs are more orange-brown. Remember: "Ochre" in the name = Orange-brown color. Both have the same squishy, gelatinous texture that separates them from other club-shaped fungi.
contextualKnowledge: There's some confusion about whether these fungi are edible - while they're often described as inedible and their common name references candy, some sources report them as decent edibles. However, their small size and gelatinous texture don't make them particularly appealing to most foragers, so they're better appreciated for their unique appearance than their culinary potential.
compareHints: Ochre Jelly Club differs from Chicken Lips mainly in color - it's more golden-orange while Chicken Lips tends toward yellow-green. The third relative, Leotia atrovirens, is much darker with more pronounced green tones. All three share that distinctive rubbery, gelatinous texture, but the warm ochre coloration makes this species the most orange-toned of the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Chicken lips can be distinguished from its close relative, the ochre jelly club, by its green cap (versus ochre/brownish) and more irregular cap shape.
